title: AI supervision: Retained responsibility is not strict liability
desc: Requires provider scrutiny, instructions and proportionate systems while distinguishing delegated error from automatic discipline.

kps.k: Delegation and AI use change how legal work is performed, not lawyers’ continuing duties of competence and supervision.
kps.d: The cluster frames outsourcing and AI-assisted practice as applications of existing professional obligations rather than exceptions to them. ABA Formal Opinion 08-451 permits outsourced legal and nonlegal support while retaining the engaging lawyer’s responsibility for competent services. Model Rules 5.1 and 5.3 distinguish firm-level safeguards from direct supervision and extend oversight beyond firm boundaries. These materials primarily supply rules and interpretive guidance, not empirical evidence that delegation improves quality or reduces costs.

qs.q: A contrary interpretation would lead to the anomalous result that lawyers who outsource have a lower standard of care when supervising outsourced lawyers than they have with respect to lawyers within their own firm.
qs.a: ABA Formal Opinion 08-451: Lawyer's Obligations When Outsourcing Legal and Nonlegal Support Services · Regulators & courts · 2008

qs.q: ## Official Comments  ### *Law Firms And Associations*\  [1]  Paragraph (a) requires lawyers with managerial authority within a law firm to make reasonable efforts to ensure that the firm has in effect measures giving reasonable assurance that nonlawyers in the firm and nonlawyers outside the firm who work on firm matters act in a way compatible with the professional obligations of the lawyer.
qs.a: ABA Model Rule 5.3: Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistance, with Official Comments · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Reasonable supervision requires proportionate systems, provider scrutiny and clear instructions—not a uniform review procedure.
kps.d: The ABA comments tailor safeguards to firm structure, practice risks and staff experience. External-provider oversight also turns on qualifications, assigned services, information-protection arrangements and jurisdictional conditions. Opinion 08-451 recommends closer scrutiny where foreign training or discipline is weak, rather than categorical exclusion, and flags document-seizure and ineffective-remedy risks. Practical measures include ethical instruction, confidentiality controls, escalation channels and review of delegated work. The Florida technology packet illustrates that assurances must sometimes establish completed protection: a vendor’s promise to sanitize a device does not suffice before disposal.

qs.q: [3] Other measures that may be required to fulfill the responsibility prescribed in paragraph (a) can depend on the firm's structure and the nature of its practice.
qs.a: ABA Model Rule 5.1: Responsibilities of Partners, Managers, and Supervisory Lawyers, with Official Comments · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: including the education, experience and reputation of the nonlawyer; the nature of the services involved; the terms of any arrangements concerning the protection of client information; and the legal and ethical environments of the jurisdictions in which the services will be performed, particularly with regard to confidentiality.
qs.a: ABA Model Rule 5.3: Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistance, with Official Comments · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Retained responsibility does not mean automatic disciplinary liability for every delegated error.
kps.d: Model Rules 5.1 and 5.3 attach responsibility for another’s misconduct to ordering or knowing ratification, or a qualifying manager’s or supervisor’s knowing failure to take timely remedial action. Separately, inadequate supervision can itself breach Rule 5.1 without knowledge of the underlying violation. Each lawyer retains personal ethical duties, and other law determines civil or criminal liability. Jurisdiction matters: the New York standard recited in Cassata also reaches misconduct a manager or supervisor reasonably should have known about, unlike the Model Rule’s stated knowledge trigger.

qs.q: [6] Professional misconduct by a lawyer under supervision could reveal a violation of paragraph (b) on the part of the supervisory lawyer even though it does not entail a violation of paragraph (c) because there was no direction, ratification or knowledge of the violation.
qs.a: ABA Model Rule 5.1: Responsibilities of Partners, Managers, and Supervisory Lawyers, with Official Comments · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: Whether a lawyer may be liable civilly or criminally for another lawyer's conduct is a question of law beyond the scope of these Rules.
qs.a: ABA Model Rule 5.1: Responsibilities of Partners, Managers, and Supervisory Lawyers, with Official Comments · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: AI guidance converges on proactive governance but differs in prescription and in how it characterises the tool.
kps.d: Oregon Opinion 2025-205 requires clear permissible-use policies and training on the actual tools, their limitations and secure data handling. D.C. Opinion 388 recommends proactive measures for foreseeable generative-AI use but presents a pre-use confidentiality requirement as an option. Joint Opinion 2024-200 argues that Rule 5.3 should apply when AI functions like a human and recommends task-specific ethical suitability assessments. The NYSBA report makes classification of tools as nonlawyers conditional; Artificially Intelligent Lawyers uses that classification only as an analytical assumption. These distinctions do not remove duties to supervise human users, and they do not establish AI’s legal status or a universal duty to adopt it.

qs.q: Managerial lawyers must establish clear policies regarding the law firm’s permissi- ble use of AI, including specifically GAI, and supervisory lawyers must make reasonable efforts to ensure that the firm’s lawyers and nonlawyers comply with their professional obligations when using such technologies.
qs.a: Oregon State Bar Formal Opinion No. 2025-205: Artificial Intelligence · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: One step law firms, lawyers, and government agencies could consider is to require employees—lawyers and nonlawyers alike—to satisfy themselves that client confidentiality under Rule 1.6 will be protected before using a GAI product.
qs.a: D.C. Bar Ethics Opinion 388: Attorneys' Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Client Matters · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Cassata gives concrete judicial force to verification, technological competence and prompt correction.
kps.d: The court found that a submission contained nonexistent decisions and quotations and unsupported legal propositions. It linked the supervising lawyer’s lack of knowledge about the newly acquired AI-enhanced Westlaw tool to inadequate supervision, finding Rule 5.1 violations by the supervisor and firm. It also found frivolous conduct and candour violations for failing to correct misstatements, and separately condemned copying another brief without verifying its authorities. The decision illustrates consequences of specific failures; it does not measure AI error rates or establish that AI caused every defect in the submission.

qs.q: First, the Court considers whether the supervising attorney, Fleming, and MMPS adequately supervised Kiousenterlis, especially in light of Kiousenterlis' submission of opposition containing nonexistent decisions, nonexistent quotations, and propositions of law that are not supported by cases cited.
qs.a: Cassata v. Michael Macrina Architect, P.C. — AI sanctions decision, Suffolk County · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: Accordingly, the Court determines that the conduct of Kiousenterlis, Fleming, and MMPS was frivolous pursuant to 22 NYCRR § 130-1.1 and violated Rule 3.3 in that they failed to promptly correct their misstatements of fact and law.
qs.a: Cassata v. Michael Macrina Architect, P.C. — AI sanctions decision, Suffolk County · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Consent and responsibility allocation depend on the service and cannot displace other legal obligations.
kps.d: Resolution 105C ordinarily recommends informed consent before retaining outside lawyers. Opinion 08-451 calls for consent when outside personnel receive protected information, while the accompanying Ethics 20/20 report leaves nonlawyer-provider consent questions for further guidance and says routine scanning or copying ordinarily needs no consent. This is a qualification, not blanket permission to disclose. Lawyers and clients should ordinarily agree who monitors client-selected providers, and firms sharing a matter should clarify scope and responsibility. Tribunal and discovery obligations survive those allocations. Supervision also does not universally cure unauthorized practice: NYC Opinion 2006-3 expressly declines that expansive interpretation.

qs.q: In addition, appropriate disclosures should be made to the client    regarding the use of lawyers or nonlawyers outside of the lawyer’s firm,    and client consent should be obtained if those lawyers or nonlawyers    will be receiving information protected by Rule 1.6.
qs.a: ABA Formal Opinion 08-451: Lawyer's Obligations When Outsourcing Legal and Nonlegal Support Services · Regulators & courts · 2008

qs.q: For example, lawyers regularly send documents to outside vendors for scanning or copying, but there is ordinarily no need to obtain the client’s consent to have those services performed.
qs.a: ABA Commission on Ethics 20/20, Resolution 105C and Report: Outsourcing · Regulators & courts · 2012

kps.k: Permission to delegate work is distinct from permission for nonlawyer ownership; Arizona changes the ownership framework while retaining lawyer-led safeguards.
kps.d: ABA Model Rule 5.4 restricts nonlawyer fee-sharing, legal-practice partnerships and ownership or leadership in specified entities, subject to exceptions, and protects independent professional judgment. Arizona’s R-20-0034 framework instead recognises licensed ABS participation by nonlawyer owners and managers and requires an identified lawyer responsible for compliance policies. These are different regulatory arrangements, not evidence about their comparative effectiveness. Arizona’s supplied amendment text interleaves old and revised language, so its reproduced fee-sharing prohibition cannot establish the final rule. The practical distinction is between expanding participation and relinquishing ethical control: the ABS framework still requires licensing, confidentiality and professional-independence safeguards.

qs.q: (c) A lawyer shall not permit a person who recommends, employs, or pays the lawyer to render legal services for another to direct or regulate the lawyer's professional judgment in rendering such legal services.
qs.a: Model Rules of Professional Conduct r. 5.4 — Professional Independence of a Lawyer · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: Any such alternative business structure (ABS) as defined in Rule 31 must be licensed in accordance with ACJA § 7-209.
qs.a: In the Matter of Restyle and Amend Rule 31; Adopt New Rule 33.1; Amend Rules 32, 41, 42 (Various ERs from 1.0 to 5.7), 46-51, 54-58, 60 and 75-76, No. R-20-0034 · Regulators & courts · 2020

vlens.an: The curated regulators, courts and professional-bodies sources accept the proposition’s core distinction: outsourcing or AI use leaves lawyers with continuing duties of competence, supervision, confidentiality and verification, but does not make them automatically disciplinarily liable for every delegated error. Their common reasoning is doctrinal rather than empirical. Existing professional rules require reasonable firm-level safeguards, direct supervision, provider scrutiny and instructions calibrated to the task, personnel, confidentiality risks and jurisdiction; derivative responsibility generally depends on direction, knowing ratification or a knowing failure to take timely remedial action. Collectively, these sources materially develop the proposition by translating it into concrete governance and enforcement: Oregon requires clear AI-use policies and tool-specific training; D.C. recommends proactive measures while treating a pre-use confidentiality check as optional; Joint Opinion 2024-200 proposes assessing AI against the ethical standard applicable to a human performing the same task; Cassata applies technological competence, verification, candour and supervision duties to an AI-assisted filing; and Arizona extends lawyer-led safeguards to licensed ABSs with nonlawyer ownership or management. Material variation remains. Cassata’s New York standard includes conduct a supervisor reasonably should have known about, broader than the Model Rules’ stated knowledge trigger. Sources also differ over whether AI should be analogised to a nonlawyer, how prescriptive governance should be, and whether nonlawyer ownership is prohibited under Model Rule 5.4 or permitted through Arizona’s licensed ABS regime. None of this establishes comparative effectiveness, measured AI reliability or a universal duty to adopt AI, and the curated set should not be treated as representative of all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

qs.q: Training must include the basics of the actual type of AI being used (rather than just AI in general), the capabilities and limitations of the tools, ethical issues in the use of that specific AI, and best practices for secure data handling, privacy, and confidentiality.
qs.a: Oregon State Bar Formal Opinion No. 2025-205: Artificial Intelligence · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: The selected academia-and-research sources support the proposition’s core: delegating work or using AI does not displace lawyers’ continuing duties of competence, supervision and confidentiality. Their common reasoning is doctrinal rather than empirical. They rely on professional rules, client expectations and disciplinary authority to treat delegation as permissible only when lawyers retain responsibility and use reasonable safeguards. They also support the proposition’s rejection of a uniform review procedure by describing supervision as dependent on circumstances such as worker experience, workload and ethical risk. Material variation lies in scope. The nonlawyer-ownership article focuses on permitted paraprofessional delegation and outsourcing, with its discussion of nonlawyer leadership largely peripheral to AI supervision. Artificially Intelligent Lawyers most directly addresses AI, but treats AI’s classification as a nonlawyer only as an analytical assumption and uses an inadequate-supervision case without fully developing the distinction between retained responsibility and automatic liability. Navigating the Power of Artificial Intelligence broadens the account to technological competence, confidentiality and firm-level compliance systems, but does not specify provider scrutiny, task-specific verification or disciplinary knowledge thresholds. Accordingly, these curated sources support rather than materially extend the synthesis, and they do not independently establish its more detailed strict-liability distinction or governance prescriptions.

qs.q: This Rule does not prohibit a lawyer from employing the services of paraprofessionals and delegating functions to them, so long as the lawyer supervises the delegated work and retains responsibility for their work.149  144.
qs.a: The Pitfalls and False Promises of Nonlawyer Ownership of Law Firms · Academia · 2022

qs.q: STATE BAR ASS’N 2009) (“[T]he degree of supervision required is that which is reasonable under the circumstances, taking into account factors such as the experience of the person whose work is being supervised, the amount of work involved in a particular matter and the likelihood that ethical problems might arise in the course of working on the matter.”).
qs.a: Artificially Intelligent Lawyers: Updating the Model Rules of Professional Conduct in Accordance with the New Technological Era · Academia · 2018

elens.an: The pre-2015 foundations support the proposition by treating outsourcing and automated services as permissible forms of delegation that leave competence, supervision and client-protection duties with the lawyer or firm. Their common rationale is that oversight should be reasonable and proportionate to the provider, task, experience, confidentiality arrangements and jurisdictional risks, rather than governed by one uniform review procedure. They also distinguish affirmative supervisory duties from automatic disciplinary responsibility for every provider error: the ABA materials attach responsibility for another’s misconduct to ordering, knowing ratification or a knowing failure to take timely remedial action. Material variation remains. The New York City opinion uses broader language of “complete professional responsibility” and expressly requires lawyers to vet quality, while the ABA framework more precisely separates reasonable safeguards from knowledge-based responsibility for specific misconduct. Formal Opinion 08-451 strongly establishes retained competence and risk-sensitive scrutiny but does not itself fully articulate the strict-liability distinction. The Ethics 20/20 materials provide the clearest bridge to the later AI proposition by expressly including automated products, although these sources concern outsourcing rather than contemporary generative AI and supply normative guidance rather than empirical evidence.

The 2015–2022 sources collectively accept the proposition’s core: delegating legal or support work does not displace lawyers’ continuing duties, and reasonable supervision varies with the circumstances. They commonly ground that conclusion in client expectations and professional-conduct rules permitting supervised paraprofessional work and outsourcing. The material extension comes from Arizona’s ABS framework, which applies lawyer-led compliance, proportionate supervision and defined responsibility triggers to licensed nonlawyer ownership, management and external assistance. It expressly ties responsibility for another’s misconduct to ordering, knowing ratification or knowing failure to take timely remedial action, reinforcing the distinction between retained responsibility and automatic discipline. Internal variation is substantial: one source principally confirms conventional delegation and outsourcing; another provisionally assumes AI is a nonlawyer without establishing its legal status; and Arizona supplies a broader regulatory architecture rather than AI-specific or empirical evidence. These curated sources therefore build on the proposition doctrinally, but do not establish the effectiveness of the safeguards or how widely these views were held during the period.

qs.q: This Rule does not prohibit a lawyer from employing the services of paraprofessionals and delegating functions to them, so long as the lawyer supervises the delegated work and retains responsibility for their work.149  144.
qs.a: The Pitfalls and False Promises of Nonlawyer Ownership of Law Firms · Academia · 2022

qs.q: (1) the lawyer orders or, with the knowledge of the specific conduct, ratifies the conduct involved; or     (2) the lawyer is a partner or has comparable managerial authority in the firm in which the person is employed, or has direct supervisory authority over the person, and knows of the conduct at a time when its consequences can be avoided or mitigated but fails to take reasonable remedial action.
qs.a: In the Matter of Restyle and Amend Rule 31; Adopt New Rule 33.1; Amend Rules 32, 41, 42 (Various ERs from 1.0 to 5.7), 46-51, 54-58, 60 and 75-76, No. R-20-0034 · Regulators & courts · 2020

elens.an: The supplied 2023–2024 sources collectively accept the proposition that generative AI changes the means of legal work without displacing lawyers’ existing duties of competence, supervision, confidentiality and verification. They also develop the proposition into a more AI-specific governance framework: foreseeable use calls for proactive safeguards, supervisors and subordinate lawyers retain independent obligations, and AI output must be checked for accuracy, completeness and confidentiality. Joint Formal Opinion 2024-200 adds the most material extension by proposing a task-specific human-equivalence test—whether the AI can satisfy the professional rules to the same extent as a human performing the same task—and by reproducing Rule 5.3’s knowledge- and conduct-based conditions for responsibility, supporting the distinction between retained responsibility and strict liability. There is meaningful variation in prescription and characterisation: D.C. Opinion 388 presents a pre-use confidentiality check as an optional measure; the NYSBA report expressly requires verification and treats classification of the tool itself as a nonlawyer conditionally; and Joint Opinion 2024-200 argues that Rule 5.3 should apply with the same force when AI functions like a human. The D.C. and NYSBA materials do not independently resolve the distinction between supervisory responsibility and automatic disciplinary liability. These conclusions describe the curated sources supplied, not the prevalence of these positions among bar authorities generally.

qs.q: Thus, when contemplating the appropriate use of generative AI, lawyers should consider whether an AI tool can satisfy the Rules of Professional Conduct to the same extent as a human hired to complete the same tasks.
qs.a: Joint Formal Opinion 2024-200 — Ethical Issues Regarding the Use of Artificial Intelligence · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources collectively accept the proposition that AI use and external assistance leave lawyers’ existing duties of competence, confidentiality and supervision in place, while responsibility for another actor’s misconduct depends on specified supervisory, knowledge, ratification or remediation conditions rather than arising automatically from every delegated error. They commonly emphasise reasonable firm-level systems, supervision of lawyers and nonlawyers, confidentiality safeguards and scrutiny extending to outside providers. The material extension comes from the Oregon opinion, which translates these general duties into concrete AI governance: clear permissible-use policies, reasonable compliance efforts and training tailored to the actual tool, its limitations, ethical risks and secure data handling. Internal variation is mainly in specificity and scope. The Florida packet most directly supports the distinction between retained responsibility and strict liability and gives a concrete example of verification beyond accepting a vendor promise. The Oregon opinion is more prescriptive about AI policies and training but does not expressly analyse strict liability. Navigating the Power of Artificial Intelligence in the Legal Field supports continuing competence, confidentiality and supervisory duties at a higher level of generality, without developing provider scrutiny, proportionate verification or liability thresholds. Because these are curated sources, their convergence should not be treated as evidence of how prevalent these views were across all 2025 legal authorities or commentators.

qs.q: Training must include the basics of the actual type of AI being used (rather than just AI in general), the capabilities and limitations of the tools, ethical issues in the use of that specific AI, and best practices for secure data handling, privacy, and confidentiality.
qs.a: Oregon State Bar Formal Opinion No. 2025-205: Artificial Intelligence · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources accept the proposition that AI use and delegation preserve duties of competence, supervision and professional independence without imposing automatic disciplinary liability for every downstream error. They materially develop it by pairing the Model Rules’ general framework with Cassata’s concrete judicial application: Rule 5.1 distinguishes reasonable supervisory systems from derivative responsibility based on direction, knowing ratification or failure to remedy known misconduct, while Cassata finds an actual supervisory violation where inadequate understanding of an AI-enhanced research tool prevented effective oversight. The principal internal variation is jurisdictional and topical. Cassata recites a New York standard extending responsibility to conduct a supervisor reasonably should have known about, broader than the Model Rule’s stated knowledge trigger. Rules 5.1 and 5.3 directly govern supervision of lawyers and nonlawyer assistance; Rule 1.1 reinforces technological competence and coordinated allocation of responsibility; and Rule 5.4 addresses the distinct issue of nonlawyer ownership, control and professional independence rather than verification or liability for delegated errors. These are predominantly normative authorities and one case application, not empirical evidence about AI reliability, the effectiveness of particular governance systems or the prevalence of these views.
